blocks.text: Нэг сая элементтэй sorted array дотроос $x$-ээс бага биш эхний элементийг олон удаа хайх хэрэгтэй боллоо. Query бүрд эхнээс нь алхвал нэг query $10^6$, $10^5$ query нийлээд $10^{11}$ орчим харьцуулалт хийнэ. Бидэнд хэрэгтэй зүйл бол хурдан loop бичихээс өмнө огт шалгах шаардлагагүй хэсгийг олох явдал.

Sorted гэдэг нь зөвхөн харагдах дараалал биш, хайхад ашиглах баталгаа юм. Голын утга $x$-ээс бага байвал түүнээс зүүн талын бүх утга ч бага. Нэг харьцуулалтаар зөвхөн нэг элементийг бус, бүхэл хэсгийг хасаж болно. Энэ хичээлээр яг байгаа эсэхээс арай ерөнхий, эхний $a_i\ge x$ заагийг олно.
$a=[2,4,4,7,9]$ дотор $x=4$-өөс бага биш хамгийн эхний утгын index-ийг олъё. Хариу $1$. Ижил утгууд байвал хамгийн эхнийхийг олох шаардлагатай.

Эхлээд linear scan зөв шийдэл мөн гэдгийг тогтоо: $a_i\ge x$ болсон эхний index дээр зогсоно, байхгүй бол $n$ буцаана. Ингээд predicate-ээ $P(i)=[a_i\ge x]$ гэж бичье. Sorted array дээр энэ нь false-уудын дараа true-ууд залгасан хэлбэртэй; false руу буцаж шилжихгүй.

Мужийн эхний index-ийг $l$, баруун заагийг $r$ гэж авна. $a[l..r)$ доторх элементүүдийг шалгах үлдсэн бөгөөд хариу зааг $r$ дээр ч байж болно. Голын $mid$ дээр true байвал $mid$-ийг хариунаас хасаж болохгүй: $r=mid$. False байвал $mid$ болон өмнөх бүгдийг хасаж $l=mid+1$ болгоно.

$l=0$, $r=n$ гэж эхэлбэл хоосон array ч тусгай if шаарддаггүй. $mid=l+(r-l)/2$ тул $l<r$ үед $l\le mid<r\le n$: код $a_n$ рүү хэзээ ч хандахгүй. Буцаасан index $n$ байвал тохирох элемент байхгүй гэсэн sentinel; түүнийг array руу шууд index болгож болохгүй.
Зүүнээс scan хийж олж болно. Харин sorted учраас дундах утга $x$-ээс бага байвал түүний зүүн талд хариу байхгүй. Нэг comparison-оор олон элементийг хасаж чадна.
Энэ ганц хичээл half-open зааг хэрэглэнэ: эхлээд $l=0,r=n$. $a[\mathrm{mid}]<x$ бол $l=\mathrm{mid}+1$. Үгүй бол mid хариу байж болох тул $r=\mathrm{mid}$. Зааг тэнцэхэд хайлт дуусна.

Эхний $a[i]\ge x$ index-ийг олохдоо array-ийн утгууд биш, “$a[i]\ge x$ үнэн үү?” гэсэн Boolean дарааллыг хар. Sorted array-д false-уудын дараа true-ууд орно. Binary search энэ шилжилтийн заагийг олно; true элемент огт байхгүй бол зааг $n$.

Loop-ийн invariant: $l$-ээс өмнөх бүх index false, $r$-ээс эхэлсэн хүчинтэй index-үүд true. $[l,r)$ доторх хэсэг хараахан шийдэгдээгүй. $a[mid]<x$ бол mid болон зүүн хэсэг false тул $l=mid+1$. Үгүй бол mid true тул $r=mid$; mid өөрөө хариу байж болохыг хадгална.

$l<r$ үед mid үргэлж хүчинтэй index бөгөөд аль branch-д ч хүрээ багасна. $l=r$ үед шийдээгүй хэсэг хоосон: энэ байрлал false ба true-ийн яг зааг. Lower bound-ийн хариу заавал $x$-тэй тэнцүү утга байх албагүй.

$a_{mid}\ge x$ бол sorted учраас түүнээс хойших бүх утга мөн нөхцөлийг хангана; $r=mid$ invariant-ийг хадгална. Харин $a_{mid}<x$ бол түүнээс өмнөх бүх утга ч бага тул $l=mid+1$ зөв. Аль ч үед $r-l$ бүхэл эерэг урт багасна, тиймээс loop заавал дуусна.

Өргөн нь $n$ байсан муж нэг алхмын дараа хамгийн ихдээ $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ орчим болно. $k$ алхмын дараа үлдсэн өргөн $n/2^k$-оос ихгүй. Эерэг бүхэл өргөн $1$-ээс бага болмогц loop дуусах тул $n>0$ үед хамгийн ихдээ $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1$ iteration хийнэ. Нэг сая элемент дээр ойролцоогоор $20$ алхам.

Iteration бүр нэг array access, нэг харьцуулалт, цөөн бүхэл тоон үйлдэлтэй тул query-ийн worst-case хугацаа $O(\log n)$. Нэмэлт зай $O(1)$; input array-ийн өөрийн зай $O(n)$. Array-г анх sort хийх хэрэгтэй бол $O(n\log n)$ preprocessing-ийг бас тооц. $q$ query-ийн нийт хугацаа $O(n\log n+q\log n)$.

Binary search нь check өөрөө үнэгүй гэсэн үг биш. Хариун дээр binary search хийж, нэг check $O(n)$ байвал нийт нь $O(n\log R)$ болно. Monotonicity байхгүй бол хурдан ажилласан ч буруу хариу гаргана. Original index хэрэгтэй бодлогод sort хийхэд index-ийн утга өөрчлөгдөхийг мөн анхаар.

Бодлогын өгүүлбэрээс “эрэмбэлсэн”, “хамгийн бага боломжит”, “хамгийн их хүрч болох” гэсэн мэдээлэл хай. Гэхдээ үг хараад алгоритм сонгохгүй: check-ээ тодорхойлоод false/true дараалал руу буцаж шилжихгүйг батал. Жижиг array дээр бүх хариуг brute force-аар гаргаж, binary search-ийн үр дүнтэй харьцуул.
Sorted lookup болон monotonic predicate-д тохирно. Equal элементүүд олон байвал энэ код эхнийхийг өгнө. Exact search хийхэд буцсан index $n$ биш, мөн тэр утга $x$-тэй тэнцүү эсэхийг нэмж шалгана.

en.title: Binary search — searching a sorted array
en.summary: Halve the search range by safely discarding an irrelevant half.

blocks.text: We repeatedly need the first element at least $x$ in a sorted array of one million values. Scanning from the start may take $10^6$ comparisons per query and about $10^{11}$ across $10^5$ queries. Before making the loop faster, ask which comparisons can be avoided entirely.

Sorted order is a guarantee we can exploit. If the middle value is below $x$, every earlier value is also below $x$. One comparison can rule out a whole region. We will find the first boundary satisfying $a_i\ge x$, which is more general than testing membership.
In $a=[2,4,4,7,9]$, find the first index whose value is at least $x=4$. The answer is $1$, even though $4$ appears twice.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: First establish a correct baseline: scan until the first index with $a_i\ge x$, or return $n$ if there is none. Write the predicate as $P(i)=[a_i\ge x]$. On sorted input it consists of false values followed by true values, with no transition back to false.

Let $l$ be the left boundary and $r$ the right boundary. The remaining array elements lie in $a[l..r)$; the answer boundary itself may equal $r$. If the middle predicate is true, keep that index as a possible answer by setting $r=mid$. If false, discard it and everything before it by setting $l=mid+1$.

Initialize $l=0$ and $r=n$; even an empty array needs no special case. With $mid=l+(r-l)/2$, the loop condition ensures $l\le mid<r\le n$, so $a_n$ is never accessed. A returned index of $n$ is a sentinel for no qualifying element and must not be dereferenced.
A left-to-right scan works, but sorted order lets us eliminate many candidates at once: if the middle value is too small, everything to its left is too small too.
This search uses half-open bounds: start with $l=0,r=n$. If $a[\mathrm{mid}]<x$, set $l=\mathrm{mid}+1$. Otherwise mid may still be the answer, so set $r=\mathrm{mid}$. Stop when the boundaries meet.

To find the first $a[i]\ge x$, view the Boolean sequence “is $a[i]\ge x$?”. In a sorted array, false positions precede true positions. Binary search locates this boundary, which is $n$ if no true position exists.

The invariant is that every index before $l$ is false and every valid index from $r$ onward is true. The undecided region is $[l,r)$. If $a[mid]<x$, move $l$ to $mid+1$; otherwise set $r=mid$, preserving mid as a possible boundary.
When $l<r$, mid is a valid index and either branch shrinks the range. At $l=r$, nothing remains undecided, so this is the exact boundary. A lower-bound result need not contain a value equal to $x$.

items: $[l,r)$ is the remaining range: $l$ is included and $r$ is excluded.
$\mathrm{mid}$ is the middle index. Return $n$ if no qualifying value exists.

blocks.text: First_at_least behaves like lower_bound. Computing $\mathrm{mid}=l+(r-l)/2$ avoids adding large bounds. If the result is $n$, do not access $a[n]$.

items: In first_at_least, $r=n$ is a sentinel boundary, not an index to read.
Computing mid as $l+(r-l)/2$ avoids overflowing $l+r$.
Using $r=mid-1$ in this half-open version can discard a valid boundary.

blocks.text: Section 13 contains a complete runnable program with the same implementation, input format and checked sample output.

Use a two-sided invariant: every index $i<l$ has $a_i<x$, and every valid index $i\ge r$ has $a_i\ge x$. Therefore the first qualifying boundary lies in $[l,r]$. Initially both assertions concern empty outside regions, so they hold.

If $a_{mid}\ge x$, sorted order makes every later value qualify, so setting $r=mid$ preserves the invariant. Otherwise every earlier value also fails, making $l=mid+1$ safe. In either case the nonnegative integer width $r-l$ strictly decreases, so the loop terminates.

At termination $l=r$. No earlier index qualifies, and if $l<n$, index $l$ does qualify. Thus $l$ is exactly the first required index. If all values were too small, the returned boundary is $n$, correctly representing failure.

items: Do not apply this search to an unsorted array.
Do not mix this half-open version with another version’s $r=\mathrm{mid}-1$ rule.

blocks.text: Once you can trace the example without looking at the code, write the implementation yourself. Compare it with a simple loop on new inputs. The links offer another explanation; this lesson’s prose, examples and code were written for Erdene Club.

The width drops to at most roughly half its previous value. After $k$ steps it is bounded by $n/2^k$. Once a nonnegative integer width is below one, it is zero. For $n>0$ there are at most $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1$ iterations: about $20$ for one million elements.

Each iteration performs one array access, one comparison and constant-size integer work, giving $O(\log n)$ worst-case query time and $O(1)$ extra space. The input array occupies $O(n)$. If sorting is needed first, include $O(n\log n)$ preprocessing; $q$ queries then cost $O(n\log n+q\log n)$ overall.

Binary search does not make the check free. Searching an answer range of width $R$ with an $O(n)$ check costs $O(n\log R)$. Without monotonicity it can be fast and still wrong. Also, sorting changes positions, so preserve original indices when the task needs them.

blocks.text: Нэг танхимд олон арга хэмжээ давхцаж байна. Аль болох олон арга хэмжээг бүтнээр нь үзэхийн тулд алийг нь сонгох вэ? Боломжит бүх subset-ийг шалгах нь зөв боловч $2^n$ сонголттой. Бид нэг сонголт хийсний дараа өмнөх бүх шийдвэрээ буцааж шалгах шаардлагагүй дүрэм хайна.

Энд арга хэмжээ бүр ижил үнэ цэнтэй, зорилго нь зөвхөн тоог ихэсгэх. “Хамгийн эрт эхэлснийг авъя” гэсэн санаа $[0,10),[1,2),[2,3)$ дээр буруу: эхнийхийг авбал нэг, сүүлийн хоёрыг авбал хоёр арга хэмжээ үзнэ. Greedy дүрмийг эхлээд эсрэг жишээгээр сорьж суръя.
Кинонуудын цаг $[1,4),[2,3),[3,5),[5,7)$ байна. Давхцахгүй хамгийн олон кино үзье. $[2,3),[3,5),[5,7)$-г сонговол $3$ кино. Нэг кино дуусах мөчид дараагийнх эхэлж болно.

Одоо боломжтой арга хэмжээнүүдээс хамгийн эрт дуусахыг сонговол дараагийн сонголтод хамгийн их зай үлдээнэ гэсэн ажиглалт хийе. Энэ бол одоохондоо intuition; дараах exchange argument л global optimum-ийг батална. Дуусах цагаар sort хийгээд одоогийн боломжит заагаас хойш эхэлж буй арга хэмжээг авна.

en.title: Greedy — making a safe choice at each step
en.summary: Learn greedy through one concrete problem and the reason its choice is safe.

blocks.text: Many events compete for one room. Which should we attend to maximize the number of complete events? Checking every subset is correct but gives $2^n$ choices. We want a rule that lets us commit to a choice without reconsidering all earlier decisions.

Every event has equal value and only the count matters. Taking the earliest start fails on $[0,10),[1,2),[2,3)$: it takes one event instead of two. A proposed greedy rule must first survive attempts to construct counterexamples.
Movies run during $[1,4),[2,3),[3,5),[5,7)$. Choose the most nonoverlapping movies. Taking $[2,3),[3,5),[5,7)$ gives $3$. A movie may start exactly when the previous one ends.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Choosing the earliest finishing available event seems to leave the most room for later choices. This is intuition, not yet a proof. The exchange argument below establishes optimality. Sort by finish time and accept events whose start is at or beyond the current availability boundary.

We use half-open intervals $[l,r)$. One event may start exactly when the previous one ends, so the condition is $l\ge lastEnd$. Closed intervals or a required break change this condition. Connect the comparator and compatibility rule to the statement rather than memorizing them.
Trying every subset gives $2^n$ possibilities. Choosing the earliest finishing available movie leaves as much room as possible for later choices.
Do not confuse earliest finish with shortest duration or earliest start. This problem specifically needs earliest finish; another greedy problem may need a different rule.
Greedy commits to a local choice without revisiting it. The objective here is the number of films, not total duration or value. Short duration is not the same selection criterion as early finishing.

Choosing the earliest finish leaves the most room for later films. Replace the first film of an optimal schedule with the earliest-finishing one: its finish cannot increase, so later films remain feasible. This exchange proves that an optimum can include the greedy choice.

Last_end stores the finish of the last accepted film. A later film is compatible when its start is no smaller. Half-open intervals $[l,r)$ permit touching endpoints, explaining the non-strict comparison.

Let $g$ be the greedy choice in the remaining problem and $o$ the first event of an optimal schedule. Since $g$ finishes earliest, $end(g)\le end(o)$. Replacing $o$ with $g$ preserves the count and cannot conflict with later events, which already started after $end(o)$.

Therefore an optimal schedule exists that starts with $g$. What remains after $g$ is the same scheduling problem on fewer events. Induction on that remaining set proves every greedy choice can be part of an optimal schedule. The safe replacement is the proof, beyond merely saying that an early finish looks good.

blocks.text: Once you can trace the example without looking at the code, write the implementation yourself. Compare it with a simple loop on new inputs. The links offer another explanation; this lesson’s prose, examples and code were written for Erdene Club.

Sorting costs $O(n\log n)$. The following scan visits each event once and performs constant work, costing $O(n)$. Together they are $O(n\log n)$; do not omit sorting and claim linear time. Only already finish-sorted input permits a linear scan alone.

This implementation takes the vector by value, so it uses an additional $O(n)$ copy besides the caller's input, plus sorting stack space. Sorting in place avoids the copy, with typical introsort using about $O(\log n)$ stack. A short function can still allocate a large copy.

The proof no longer applies when events carry weights and total weight is the objective. Events $[0,3),[3,6)$ of weight $2$ each beat a weight-$100$ event $[0,6)$ by count but not by weight. The exchange does not preserve the objective, so another method such as DP is needed.

State-аа бүтэн өгүүлбэрээр тодорхойл: $dp_i$ нь яг $i$ гишгүүрийг туулах алхмын дарааллын тоо. Ирээдүйн боломжийг шийдэхэд өмнөх алхмуудын бүх түүх биш, үлдсэн зай л хэрэгтэй. Энэ нь ижил state-уудыг нэгтгэж болох шалтгаан.

DP-г formula цээжлэхээс биш state-ийн утга бичихээс эхэл. Энд $dp[i]$ нь яг $i$ гишгүүр хүрэх ordered алхмын дарааллын тоо. $1,2$ ба $2,1$ өөр зам. Зөвхөн сүүлийн хэдэн алхмыг мэдэхэд цаашдын боломж бүрэн тодорхой болох state сонгоно.

en.title: Introduction to DP — saving smaller answers
en.summary: Learn states, base cases and transitions one at a time through a stair problem.

blocks.text: You climb a staircase of $n$ steps, moving up by $1$ or $2$ each time. How many sequences reach the top? For $n=4$ they are $1+1+1+1$, $1+1+2$, $1+2+1$, $2+1+1$, and $2+2$. First establish that order matters: $1+2$ and $2+1$ are different sequences.

Generating every sequence recursively is correct. However, the same problem with five steps remaining is solved again whenever a different prefix reaches it. DP is useful because those residual problems repeat, not simply because recursion is present.
Climb $n$ stairs using steps of size one or two. For $n=3$, the routes are $1+1+1$, $1+2$, and $2+1$: three ways. What about larger $n$?

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Define the state in a full sentence: $dp_i$ counts sequences that climb exactly $i$ steps. Future possibilities depend on the remaining distance, not the entire earlier history. That is why different paths reaching the same state can share one computed answer.

Classify sequences by their final move. Those ending in $1$ correspond to a sequence reaching $i-1$ followed by $1$; those ending in $2$ correspond to one reaching $i-2$ followed by $2$. Hence $dp_i=dp_{i-1}+dp_{i-2}$, with the second term included only for $i\ge2$.

Set $dp_0=1$: the empty sequence is one way to climb zero steps. Setting it to zero corrupts every later answer. Processing increasing $i$ ensures all smaller dependencies are ready; that dependency order is the basis of bottom-up DP.
A recursion can split by the final step, but repeatedly recomputes the same smaller answers. Save those answers in an array.
A final step of one comes from $i-1$; a final step of two comes from $i-2$. These groups do not overlap, so add their counts: $\mathrm{dp}[i]=\mathrm{dp}[i-1]+\mathrm{dp}[i-2]$.

Start DP by defining a state rather than memorizing a formula. Here $dp[i]$ counts ordered step sequences reaching exactly stair $i$. Sequences $1,2$ and $2,1$ are different. A state must contain all information needed for future choices.
The last step is $1$ or $2$. The first group extends paths to $i-1$ by $1$; the second extends paths to $i-2$ by $2$. Their last steps differ, so the groups are disjoint: $dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]$.

Base case $dp[0]$=$1$ represents the single empty path. It lets early answers follow the same recurrence. Increasing $i$ ensures dependencies are ready. Memoization computes states on demand through recursion; tabulation fills them in a chosen order.

blocks.text: Section 13 contains a complete runnable program with the same implementation, input format and checked sample output.

The base case at $i=0$ is correct. Assume every smaller state is correct. Every valid sequence ends with either $1$ or $2$, so those two groups cover all possibilities. Different final moves make the groups disjoint.

Removing the final move leaves exactly one sequence in the corresponding smaller state. Conversely, appending that move to any smaller-state sequence creates one valid sequence. This bijection proves the transition counts, and induction establishes $dp_n$.

Modulo does not preserve the exact count, but it preserves the requested residue: $(a+b)\bmod M=((a\bmod M)+(b\bmod M))\bmod M$. Counts grow quickly, so taking the modulus only at the end may be too late to prevent overflow.

blocks.text: Once you can trace the example without looking at the code, write the implementation yourself. Compare it with a simple loop on new inputs. The links offer another explanation; this lesson’s prose, examples and code were written for Erdene Club.

Naive recursion recomputes states and creates exponentially many calls, bounded above by $O(2^n)$. DP has $n+1$ states. It reads one dependency for $i=1$ and only two thereafter, giving $O(n)$ work. The speedup comes from evaluating each state once, not from the label DP.

The program stores $n+1$ long long values, taking $O(n)$ space or roughly $8(n+1)$ bytes. For the final count alone, only the last two states are needed, allowing $O(1)$ extra space. Do not discard the array blindly when reconstruction or multiple-state answers are required.

If $n$ is as large as $10^{18}$, linear time is still too slow. This recurrence admits faster methods such as matrix exponentiation. Always count states, transition cost per state, preprocessing and memory instead of assuming every DP fits every constraint.

sections.title: 13. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Ask which facts about a chosen prefix can affect the future. If the previous chosen colour matters, an index alone is insufficient. Before merging histories into one state, check that they really have the same possible continuations.

Minimization, maximization and counting require different bases and unreachable values. Counting often uses zero where minimization needs $INF$. Writing the state sentence and transition proof before code reveals incorrect initialization and double counting early.

For counting, minimum-cost and maximum-score DP, first define state, transition, base and evaluation order. Minimum DP often needs INF for unreachable states rather than zero. If identical states have different future options, the state definition is incomplete.
